keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Celebrates God's victory from Zion over the weapons of war.

keyThemes.explanation: God breaks the bow, shield, sword, and battle itself.
God arose to judgment to save the meek of the earth.
All who are round about him are called to fear him and bring him gifts.

Psalms 77.summary: In his day of trouble the psalmist cries to God, and "my soul refused to be comforted," asking, "Will the Lord cast off for ever? ... Hath God forgotten to be gracious?" (Psalm 77:2,7,9). He resolves to "remember the works of the LORD" and "thy wonders of old," recalling how "the waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid" (Psalm 77:11,16). He ends, "Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron," though "thy footsteps are not known" (Psalm 77:19-20).
Psalms 77.whereWeAre: Psalm 76 celebrated a victory God had already won. Psalm 77 turns to present trouble: the psalmist cries to God, finds no comfort, and asks, "Will the Lord cast off for ever?" before choosing to remember "the years of the right hand of the most High" (Psalm 77:1-2,7,10). Psalm 78 widens that remembering into a long recital of Israel's history for the next generation.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Led Israel through the sea like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron, though his way is hidden (Psalm 77:19-20).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Moves from despair to remembering God's past wonders.

keyThemes.explanation: The psalmist's present trouble leads him to remember God's past deeds instead of despair.
He meditates on the exodus, when God led his people like a flock.
God's path through the sea left no visible footsteps.

Psalms 78.summary: Asaph calls Israel to teach the next generation "the praises of the LORD... that they might set their hope in God" (Psalm 78:4,7). Despite manna from heaven and water from the rock, the people "sinned yet more" and "limited the Holy One of Israel" in the wilderness (Psalm 78:17,41). Because of continued rebellion God "forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh" and let the ark be captured, but then "chose the tribe of Judah" and "David also his servant" to shepherd his people (Psalm 78:60,67-68,70-71).
Psalms 78.whereWeAre: Psalm 77 ended by remembering the exodus. Psalm 78 extends that memory into a long history for the next generation, from the exodus and wilderness rebellions to the fall of Shiloh and God's choice of David as shepherd-king (Psalm 78:5-7,60,70-71). Psalm 79 follows with a lament over Jerusalem and its temple in ruins.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Fed Israel with manna in the wilderness, judged their rebellion at Shiloh, and chose David to shepherd his people (Psalm 78:24,60,70).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Retells Israel's history so the next generation will set their hope in God.

keyFigures.name: Israel's ancestors
keyFigures.role: Repeatedly rebel and forget God's wonders despite his provision in the wilderness (Psalm 78:17-19,40-42,56-57).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Chosen by God from tending sheep to shepherd Jacob, God's people (Psalm 78:70-72).

keyThemes.explanation: Children are to be taught God's praises and works so they will set their hope in him.
Israel's ancestors tested God repeatedly despite his provision in the wilderness.
God fed his people with manna but also judged their unfaithfulness at Shiloh.

explainedReferences.explanation: About speaking in parables.
The crowd quotes Scripture concerning bread from heaven.

Psalms 79.summary: Asaph laments, "the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps," with the dead left unburied (Psalm 79:1-3). He asks, "How long, LORD? wilt thou be angry for ever?" and pleads, "remember not against us former iniquities... help us, O God of our salvation" (Psalm 79:5,8-9). He asks God to repay the neighboring nations "sevenfold," promising, "we thy people... will give thee thanks for ever" (Psalm 79:12-13).
Psalms 79.whereWeAre: Psalm 78 recalled Shiloh's fall after Israel's rebellion. Psalm 79 laments a later disaster: "the heathen are come into thine inheritance... they have laid Jerusalem on heaps" (Psalm 79:1), asking God to forgive his people and repay their enemies. Psalm 80 continues the lament, picturing Israel as a vine God must restore.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to forgive his people's sins and to repay the nations who defiled his temple and city (Psalm 79:8-9,12).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Laments the ruined temple and city and pleads for mercy.

keyFigures.name: The heathen
keyFigures.role: Defiled God's temple, laid Jerusalem in ruins, and left the dead unburied (Psalm 79:1-3).

keyThemes.explanation: Enemies have destroyed the temple and left Jerusalem in ruins.
The psalmist asks God not to remember former iniquities but to show mercy.
He promises that God's people will give thanks forever once delivered.

Psalms 80.summary: The psalmist calls to the "Shepherd of Israel," who "leadest Joseph like a flock" and "dwellest between the cherubims," to "shine forth" and save (Psalm 80:1-2). He recalls how God "brought a vine out of Egypt" and planted it so it filled the land, but now its hedges are broken down and it is "burned with fire" (Psalm 80:8,12,16). Three times he repeats, "Turn us again, O God... and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved" (Psalm 80:3,7,19).
Psalms 80.whereWeAre: Psalm 79 lamented Jerusalem's ruin. Psalm 80 pictures Israel as a vine God brought "out of Egypt" and planted, now broken down and burned, pleading three times, "Turn us again, O God... and we shall be saved" (Psalm 80:8,16,19). Psalm 81 answers with God's own voice recalling the exodus and calling Israel to listen.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Called the Shepherd of Israel who once planted the vine of his people and is asked to turn and save them again (Psalm 80:1,8,19).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Pleads for God to restore the vine he once planted.

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Pictured as a vine God brought out of Egypt, now broken down and burned (Psalm 80:8,12,16).

keyThemes.explanation: God is called the Shepherd of Israel who leads his people like a flock.
Israel, pictured as a vine brought from Egypt, is broken down and burned.
The repeated refrain asks God to turn his people back and save them.

Psalms 81.summary: The festival calls for trumpet and timbrel, for it is "a statute for Israel... when he went out through the land of Egypt" (Psalm 81:3-5). God recalls, "I removed his shoulder from the burden," and warns, "There shall no strange god be in thee; neither shalt thou worship any strange god" (Psalm 81:6,9). Because "my people would not hearken to my voice," he "gave them up unto their own hearts' lust," but wishes, "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me," for then he would have fed them "with the finest of the wheat" (Psalm 81:11-13,16).
Psalms 81.whereWeAre: Psalm 80 pleaded for restoration. Psalm 81 answers in God's own voice, recalling how he freed Israel's "shoulder... from the burden" in Egypt and proved them at the waters of Meribah, warning, "there shall no strange god be in thee" (Psalm 81:6-7,9). Psalm 82 turns from Israel's worship to God's judgment of unjust rulers.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Freed Israel from Egypt's burden, warns against strange gods, and laments that his people would not listen (Psalm 81:6,9-11).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Recalls the exodus and God's warning against strange gods.

keyThemes.explanation: God recalls freeing Israel's shoulder from the burden in Egypt.
God warns against strange gods and calls Israel to hearken to his voice.
Because Israel would not listen, God gave them up to their own hearts' lust.

Psalms 82.summary: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods," asking rulers, "How long will ye judge unjustly?" (Psalm 82:1-2). He commands them, "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy," for they "know not, neither will they understand" (Psalm 82:3,5). Though he had said, "Ye are gods," they "shall die like men," and the psalm ends asking God himself to "arise" and "judge the earth" (Psalm 82:6-8).
Psalms 82.whereWeAre: Psalm 81 lamented that Israel would not listen to God. Psalm 82 turns to unjust rulers, pictured standing before God "in the congregation of the mighty," rebuked for failing to "defend the poor and fatherless" though he had called them, "Ye are gods" (Psalm 82:1,3,6) — words Jesus later quotes in John 10:34. Psalm 83 follows with a plea against a coalition of enemy nations.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Stands in judgment over unjust rulers, calling them to defend the poor and warning they will die like men (Psalm 82:1,3,6-7).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Condemns rulers who fail to defend the poor and fatherless.

keyFigures.name: The unjust rulers
keyFigures.role: Judge unjustly, favor the wicked, and fail to defend the poor and fatherless (Psalm 82:2-4).

keyThemes.explanation: Rulers are commanded to defend the poor, fatherless, and afflicted.
Though called gods, unjust rulers will still die like ordinary men.
The psalm ends asking God himself to rise and judge the whole earth.

explainedReferences.explanation: The words 'Ye are gods'.

Psalms 83.summary: Enemies "have taken crafty counsel" and said, "let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance" (Psalm 83:3-4). The psalmist names the coalition — Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, the Philistines, Tyre, and Assur — and asks God to defeat them as he defeated Midian and Sisera at the brook of Kison (Psalm 83:6-9). He asks that they be made "like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind," so that "men may know" that God "alone is JEHOVAH... the most high over all the earth" (Psalm 83:13,18).
Psalms 83.whereWeAre: Psalm 82 asked God to judge the whole earth. Psalm 83 names a specific threat: a coalition of nations — Edom, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre, and others — who "consulted together" to "cut them off from being a nation" (Psalm 83:4-8). Psalm 84 turns from this threatened war to a quiet pilgrim's longing for God's courts.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to scatter the enemy coalition as he once defeated Midian and Sisera, so all will know he alone is JEHOVAH (Psalm 83:9-10,18).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Names the nations conspiring against Israel and asks God to defeat them.

keyFigures.name: The enemy coalition
keyFigures.role: Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Tyre, and others who conspire to erase Israel as a nation (Psalm 83:4-8).

keyThemes.explanation: Named nations conspire together to erase Israel's name.
The psalmist recalls past victories over Midian and Sisera as a pattern for this prayer.
The goal of the prayer is that all nations know God alone is the Most High.

Psalms 84.summary: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" the psalmist cries, for "my soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD" (Psalm 84:1-2). Even sparrows nest near God's altars, and those who pass through "the valley of Baca" find it turned into "a well" (Psalm 84:3,6). "A day in thy courts is better than a thousand," he says, for "I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness" (Psalm 84:10).
Psalms 84.whereWeAre: Psalm 83 asked God to defeat Israel's enemies. Psalm 84 turns to quiet longing for God's own house: "My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD" (Psalm 84:2), preferring to be "a doorkeeper in the house of my God" over any comfort elsewhere. Psalm 85 continues with thanks for a restored land.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: A sun and shield who gives grace and glory and withholds no good thing from the upright (Psalm 84:11).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalmist's soul faints with longing for God's courts.
Even the dry valley of Baca becomes a well for those traveling to Zion.
A single day near God is valued above a thousand elsewhere, even as a mere doorkeeper.

Psalms 85.summary: "LORD, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob," forgiving their iniquity (Psalm 85:1-2). The psalmist asks, "Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?" and waits to hear God "speak peace unto his people" (Psalm 85:6,8). "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other," and "righteousness shall go before him" (Psalm 85:10,13).
Psalms 85.whereWeAre: Psalm 84 longed for God's courts. Psalm 85 gives thanks that God has already "brought back the captivity of Jacob" and forgiven his people's sin, while asking him to "revive us again" so that "mercy and truth" may meet (Psalm 85:1-2,6,10). Psalm 86 follows with David's own personal prayer for mercy.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Has forgiven his people's sin and is asked to revive them again, bringing mercy, truth, righteousness, and peace together (Psalm 85:1-2,6,10).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: God has already forgiven his people's sin and restored the land.
Mercy, truth, righteousness, and peace are pictured meeting together.
The psalmist asks that the land once more yield its increase.

Psalms 86.summary: David prays, "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy," trusting that God is "ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy" (Psalm 86:1,5). He asks, "Teach me thy way, O LORD... unite my heart to fear thy name," calling God "a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering" (Psalm 86:11,15). He ends asking for "a token for good," that those who hate him may see it and be ashamed, "because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me" (Psalm 86:17).
Psalms 86.whereWeAre: Psalm 85 was a communal prayer for revival. Psalm 86, the only psalm titled simply "A Prayer of David" in Book Three, is personal: "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy" (Psalm 86:1), asking God to "unite my heart to fear thy name" (Psalm 86:11). Psalm 87 turns from this personal prayer to praise for Zion as a city for all nations.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Ready to forgive and plenteous in mercy, asked to unite David's heart and show him a token for good (Psalm 86:5,11,17).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays as one poor and needy for an undivided heart and deliverance from enemies.

keyThemes.explanation: David asks God to teach him his way and unite his heart.
He promises to praise God with all his heart forever.
Proud and violent men rise against him, but God is full of compassion.

Psalms 87.summary: "His foundation is in the holy mountains," for "the LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob" (Psalm 87:1-2). God names Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia and says of each, "this man was born there," as if Zion were their birthplace too (Psalm 87:4). "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people," and singers and players alike will say, "all my springs are in thee" (Psalm 87:6-7).
Psalms 87.whereWeAre: Psalm 86 was David's personal prayer. Psalm 87 widens to praise Zion itself, "the city of God," where people born in Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia are counted as citizens, "this man was born there" (Psalm 87:3-4). Psalm 88 follows with the Bible's bleakest lament, offering no such comfort.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Loves Zion above every other dwelling and counts people from foreign nations as citizens born there (Psalm 87:2,4,6).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: Zion is praised as the city God loves above every dwelling of Jacob.
People from Egypt, Babylon, and other nations are counted as if born in Zion.
Singers declare that all their joy is found in Zion.

Psalms 88.summary: Heman cries, "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee," for his "soul is full of troubles" and he is "counted with them that go down into the pit" (Psalm 88:1,3-4). God has "laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps" and put "mine acquaintance far from me" (Psalm 88:6,8). The psalm ends without relief: "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness" (Psalm 88:18).
Psalms 88.whereWeAre: Psalm 87 praised Zion as a joyful home for many nations. Psalm 88 is the Bible's bleakest prayer, crying "day and night" from what feels like "the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps," and unlike almost every other psalm it ends without any turn to praise or hope (Psalm 88:1,6,18). Psalm 89 follows by returning to God's covenant promise to David, which this same darkness seems to contradict.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Called the God of the psalmist's salvation even though he seems to have laid him in the darkest pit (Psalm 88:1,6).

keyFigures.name: Heman the Ezrahite
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist; one of the wise men named alongside Solomon (1 Kings 4:31). Cries out from deep darkness and isolation with no resolution.

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Also named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: Unlike most psalms, this one ends in darkness without any turn to hope.
Friends and acquaintances are put far from him in his affliction.
He keeps crying out day and night despite receiving no answer.

Psalms 89.summary: Ethan praises God's "mercies" and recalls his covenant with David: "Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations" (Psalm 89:1,3-4). God himself speaks of finding David his servant, promising that even if his children sin, "my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail" (Psalm 89:20,33). Yet now, he says, "thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed," asking, "LORD, where are thy former lovingkindnesses, which thou swarest unto David" (Psalm 89:38,49), before the psalm, and Book Three, ends, "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen" (Psalm 89:52).
Psalms 89.whereWeAre: Psalm 88 ended in unrelieved darkness. Psalm 89 returns to God's covenant with David, praising his mercies and faithfulness before asking how that covenant and the king's present humiliation fit together, ending Book Three: "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen" (Psalm 89:52). Book Four opens with Psalm 90's prayer of Moses, "LORD, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations."

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Made an everlasting covenant with David and is now asked where his former lovingkindnesses have gone (Psalm 89:3-4,49).

keyFigures.name: Ethan the Ezrahite
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist; one of the wise men named alongside Solomon (1 Kings 4:31). Praises God's covenant with David and laments its apparent collapse.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: God's chosen servant and anointed king, promised an everlasting throne, whose crown is now described as cast to the ground (Psalm 89:20,39).

keyThemes.explanation: God swears an everlasting covenant to establish David's throne.
The anointed king's crown and strongholds now lie broken.
The psalm ends asking how long God's former lovingkindnesses will seem absent.

Psalms 90.summary: Moses declares, "LORD, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations," for God is God "from everlasting to everlasting" (Psalm 90:1-2). Human life is brief: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten... it is soon cut off, and we fly away" (Psalm 90:10). He prays, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom," asking God to "establish thou the work of our hands" (Psalm 90:12,17).
Psalms 90.whereWeAre: Psalm 89 ended Book Three asking where God's former lovingkindnesses had gone. Psalm 90, the only psalm attributed to Moses, opens Book Four by widening the lens: "LORD, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations," even though human life is brief, "for it is soon cut off, and we fly away" (Psalm 90:1,10). Psalm 91 answers with a song of refuge under God's wings.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Has been Israel's dwelling place in every generation, existing from everlasting to everlasting (Psalm 90:1-2).

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist; the only psalm attributed to him. Contrasts God's eternity with the brevity of human life and asks for wisdom.

keyThemes.explanation: God existed before the mountains were formed and remains from everlasting to everlasting.
Human life is compared to grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening.
Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days so they gain a wise heart.

Psalms 91.summary: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty," delivered "from the snare of the fowler" and the pestilence (Psalm 91:1,3). "He shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways" (Psalm 91:11) — words later quoted by the devil tempting Jesus (Matthew 4:6). God himself speaks the closing promise: "Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him... with long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation" (Psalm 91:14,16).
Psalms 91.whereWeAre: Psalm 90 prayed for wisdom in a brief life. Psalm 91 answers with assurance: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty," safe from "the pestilence that walketh in darkness" (Psalm 91:1,6) — words the devil later quotes when tempting Jesus (Psalm 91:11-12; Matthew 4:6). Psalm 92 follows with a sabbath song of thanksgiving.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: A refuge and fortress who gives his angels charge to protect the one who trusts him, and promises deliverance and long life (Psalm 91:2,11,14-16).

keyThemes.explanation: Whoever dwells in God's secret place abides safely under his protection.
God promises protection from hidden snares, plague, and attacking enemies.
God speaks in the first person, promising to deliver and satisfy the one who loves him.

explainedReferences.explanation: The tempter quotes the psalm about angels providing protection.
The tempter quotes the psalm about angels guarding someone.

Psalms 92.summary: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD," showing his lovingkindness "in the morning" and faithfulness "every night" (Psalm 92:1-2). Though "the wicked spring as the grass... they shall be destroyed for ever," the psalmist's horn is exalted and he is "anointed with fresh oil" (Psalm 92:7,10). "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon," still bringing forth fruit "in old age" (Psalm 92:12,14).
Psalms 92.whereWeAre: Psalm 91 promised protection for those who trust God. Psalm 92, the only psalm titled for the sabbath day, gives thanks that "the wicked spring as the grass" only to be "destroyed for ever," while "the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree" (Psalm 92:7,12). Psalm 93 continues the praise, declaring, "The LORD reigneth."

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Destroys the wicked, who flourish only briefly, while causing the righteous to flourish like palm trees and cedars (Psalm 92:7,12).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalm gives thanks for God's lovingkindness every morning and night.
The wicked flourish only briefly before being destroyed forever.
The righteous are compared to palm trees and cedars that keep bearing fruit even in old age.

Psalms 93.summary: "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty... the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved" (Psalm 93:1). "The floods have lifted up... their voice," but "the LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters" (Psalm 93:3-4). "Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O LORD, for ever" (Psalm 93:5).
Psalms 93.whereWeAre: Psalm 92 gave thanks for God's enduring reign over the wicked. Psalm 93 opens a series of psalms celebrating God as king (Psalms 93, 96-99): "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty," mightier than the roaring floods (Psalm 93:1,4). Psalm 94 turns from this kingship to a cry against injustice still unpunished on earth.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Reigns clothed in majesty and strength, mightier than the roaring floods and the waves of the sea (Psalm 93:1,4).

keyThemes.explanation: God reigns, clothed with majesty, his throne established from everlasting.
God is mightier than the roaring floods, an ancient symbol of chaos.
God's testimonies are sure, and holiness belongs to his house forever.

Psalms 94.summary: The psalmist asks, "LORD, how long shall the wicked... triumph?" for they slay "the widow and the stranger" and say, "The LORD shall not see" (Psalm 94:3,6-7). He answers, "He that planted the ear, shall he not hear?" and calls blessed "the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD" (Psalm 94:9,12). "Unless the LORD had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence," he confesses, "the LORD is my defence; and my God is the rock of my refuge" (Psalm 94:17,22).
Psalms 94.whereWeAre: Psalm 93 declared that God reigns. Psalm 94 asks how long the wicked will "triumph," slaying "the widow and the stranger" while saying, "The LORD shall not see" (Psalm 94:3,6-7), before trusting, "Unless the LORD had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence" (Psalm 94:17). Psalm 95 calls worshipers to come before this same God with singing.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hears and sees despite the wicked's denial, disciplines those he loves, and is the psalmist's defence and refuge (Psalm 94:9,12,22).

keyFigures.name: The wicked
keyFigures.role: Triumph for a time, slaying the widow, stranger, and fatherless, while denying that God sees (Psalm 94:3,6-7).

keyThemes.explanation: The wicked oppress the vulnerable while boasting that God does not see.
God who made the ear and eye surely sees and disciplines those he loves.
When the psalmist's foot nearly slips, God's mercy and comfort hold him up.

explainedReferences.explanation: The statement that the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise are vain.

Psalms 95.summary: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD... let us kneel before the LORD our maker," for "we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand" (Psalm 95:1,6-7). "To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your heart, as in the provocation... in the wilderness," he warns, recalling how Israel's fathers "tempted me, proved me, and saw my work" (Psalm 95:7-9). God swore in his wrath concerning that generation, "they should not enter into my rest" (Psalm 95:11).
Psalms 95.whereWeAre: Psalm 94 trusted God as a refuge from injustice. Psalm 95 calls worshipers to "come before his presence with thanksgiving" and "kneel before the LORD our maker," then warns, "To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your heart, as in the provocation" at Meribah (Psalm 95:2,6-8) — a warning Hebrews later quotes at length (Hebrews 3-4). Psalm 96 answers with a new song calling all the earth to worship.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Israel's maker and shepherd, who swore that the generation that hardened its heart in the wilderness would not enter his rest (Psalm 95:6-7,11).

keyThemes.explanation: Worshipers are called to sing and kneel before God as their maker.
Israel is described as the sheep of God's own pasture and hand.
The psalm warns against hardening the heart today as Israel did at Meribah.

explainedReferences.explanation: The warning against hardening hearts in the wilderness.
The exhortation not to harden hearts when hearing God's voice.

Psalms 96.summary: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth... declare his glory among the heathen" (Psalm 96:1,3). "All the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens," so the psalmist calls for an offering to be brought into his courts (Psalm 96:5,8). "Say among the heathen that the LORD reigneth," and let all creation rejoice, "for he cometh to judge the earth" (Psalm 96:10,13).
Psalms 96.whereWeAre: Psalm 95 warned against hardening the heart. Psalm 96 answers with "a new song," much of it sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23-33), declaring, "all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens" (Psalm 96:5). Psalm 97 continues celebrating God's reign with fire, lightning, and melting hills.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Made the heavens, unlike the idols of the nations, and comes to judge the earth with righteousness (Psalm 96:5,13).

keyThemes.explanation: All the earth and every family of peoples are called to sing to God.
The gods of the nations are called idols, unlike the LORD who made the heavens.
Creation itself rejoices because God comes to judge the world in righteousness.

Psalms 97.summary: "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice," for "clouds and darkness are round about him" and "a fire goeth before him" (Psalm 97:1-3). "The hills melted like wax at the presence of the LORD," and "confounded be all they that serve graven images" (Psalm 97:5,7). "Ye that love the LORD, hate evil," for "light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart" (Psalm 97:10-11).
Psalms 97.whereWeAre: Psalm 96 called all the earth to worship. Psalm 97 pictures that reign with the imagery of Sinai, clouds, fire, and lightning, as "the hills melted like wax at the presence of the LORD," while idol-worshipers are put to shame (Psalm 97:5,7). Psalm 98 continues with a new song for the coming judge.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Reigns with fire, lightning, and melting hills, putting idol-worshipers to shame while sowing light for the righteous (Psalm 97:3,5,7,11).

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD's reign is pictured with clouds, darkness, and a throne built on righteousness.
Those who serve graven images are put to shame before God.
Light and gladness are sown for the righteous and upright in heart.

Psalms 98.summary: "O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory" (Psalm 98:1). He "hath remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel," so "all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God" (Psalm 98:3). The psalm calls for trumpets and singing, "let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together... for he cometh to judge the earth" (Psalm 98:6,8-9).
Psalms 98.whereWeAre: Psalm 97 pictured God's reign in storm imagery. Psalm 98 answers with a gentler new song, for "his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory," remembering "his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel" (Psalm 98:1,3) — words Isaac Watts later drew on for the hymn Joy to the World. Psalm 99 continues the series of kingship psalms, now from the throne above the cherubim.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Wins victory by his own right hand and remembers his mercy to Israel, coming to judge the earth with righteousness (Psalm 98:1,3,9).

keyThemes.explanation: A new song celebrates the victory God has won by his own strength.
God's righteousness and salvation are shown openly before all nations.
The sea, floods, and hills are pictured joining in joyful praise.

Psalms 99.summary: "The LORD reigneth; let the people tremble: he sitteth between the cherubims," for "the LORD is great in Zion" (Psalm 99:1-2). "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name... they called upon the LORD, and he answered them" (Psalm 99:6). "Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions" (Psalm 99:8).
Psalms 99.whereWeAre: Psalm 98 celebrated God's victory. Psalm 99 pictures him enthroned "between the cherubims," naming "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name" as those who called on God and were answered (Psalm 99:1,6). Psalm 100 follows with a short, joyful call to thanksgiving.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Enthroned between the cherubim, great in Zion, a God who answered Moses, Aaron, and Samuel when they called (Psalm 99:1-2,6).

keyFigures.name: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel
keyFigures.role: Named as those among God's priests and those who called on his name and were answered (Psalm 99:6).

keyThemes.explanation: God reigns enthroned between the cherubim, great and holy in Zion.
The king's strength is tied to loving judgment and establishing equity in Jacob.
Worshipers are called to exalt God and bow at his footstool and holy hill.

Psalms 100.summary: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing" (Psalm 100:1-2). "Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture" (Psalm 100:3). "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving... for the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations" (Psalm 100:4-5).
Psalms 100.whereWeAre: Psalm 99 named those God answered in ages past. Psalm 100, titled "A Psalm of praise" (in Hebrew, a psalm for thanksgiving), calls all lands to "enter into his gates with thanksgiving," for "the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us" (Psalm 100:3-4). Psalm 101 turns from corporate worship to a king's personal vow of integrity.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Made his people, who are called the sheep of his pasture; his mercy is everlasting and his truth endures (Psalm 100:3,5).

keyThemes.explanation: All lands are called to serve the LORD with gladness and singing.
God's people belong to him as the sheep of his own pasture.
God's goodness, mercy, and truth endure to every generation.

Psalms 101.summary: David vows, "I will sing of mercy and judgment... I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way," walking within his own house "with a perfect heart" (Psalm 101:1-2). He resolves, "Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off," and, "He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house" (Psalm 101:5,7). He ends, "I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the LORD" (Psalm 101:8).
Psalms 101.whereWeAre: Psalm 100 was a call to corporate worship. Psalm 101 turns personal: David, the king, vows, "I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way... I will walk within my house with a perfect heart," rejecting slander and deceit from his court (Psalm 101:2-3,7). Psalm 102 follows with the very different voice of someone afflicted and overwhelmed.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The one David sings to and whose city he vows to keep free of slander, deceit, and wickedness (Psalm 101:1,8).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the king and psalmist. Vows personal integrity and promises to remove the wicked from his household and city.

keyThemes.explanation: David vows to walk with a perfect heart both personally and within his own house.
He resolves to cut off anyone who secretly slanders a neighbor.
He will keep the deceitful and proud out of his own house and service.

Psalms 102.summary: The afflicted cries, "Hear my prayer, O LORD... Hide not thy face from me in the day when I am in trouble" (Psalm 102:1-2). He feels "like a pelican of the wilderness... like an owl of the desert," his days "consumed like smoke" (Psalm 102:3,6). Yet he trusts, "Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her... is come," for though the earth and heavens "shall perish," God endures: "thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end" (Psalm 102:13,26-27).
Psalms 102.whereWeAre: Psalm 101 was a king's vow of integrity. Psalm 102, "A Prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed," is the opposite: a sufferer who feels like "a pelican of the wilderness" and whose "days are like a shadow," yet who trusts that God "shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion" (Psalm 102:6,11,13). Psalm 103 answers with exuberant blessing instead of lament.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Endures forever even as heaven and earth wear out like a garment, and will arise to rebuild Zion (Psalm 102:13,26-27).

keyThemes.explanation: The afflicted cries out, comparing himself to a lonely pelican, owl, and sparrow.
He trusts that God will arise and have mercy on Zion in his own appointed time.
Heaven and earth wear out like a garment, but God's years have no end.

explainedReferences.explanation: Declaration about the Creator remaining when creation changes.

Psalms 103.summary: David calls, "Bless the LORD, O my soul... who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases," for "the LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy" (Psalm 103:1,3,8). "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us," and "like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him," for "he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust" (Psalm 103:12-14). He ends calling angels, hosts, and all God's works to "bless the LORD, O my soul" (Psalm 103:20-22).
Psalms 103.whereWeAre: Psalm 102 cried out in affliction. Psalm 103 answers with exuberant blessing: David calls his own soul to "bless the LORD," who "forgiveth all thine iniquities" and is "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy," echoing God's own words to Moses (Psalm 103:1,3,8; Exodus 34:6). Psalm 104 widens that praise from God's mercy to his care over all creation.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Merciful and gracious, forgiving iniquity and healing disease, pitying his people as a father pities his children (Psalm 103:3,8,13).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Calls his own soul, and then all creation, to bless the LORD.

keyThemes.explanation: God forgives iniquity and removes transgressions as far as east is from west.
God remembers that human life is as brief and fragile as grass or a flower.
Angels, heavenly hosts, and all God's works everywhere are called to bless him.

Psalms 104.summary: "Bless the LORD, O my soul. O LORD my God, thou art very great," clothed with honour and majesty, stretching "out the heavens like a curtain" (Psalm 104:1-2). He sends springs to water wild donkeys, gives "wine that maketh glad the heart of man" and bread, and lets even "the young lions roar after their prey" seeking their food "from God" (Psalm 104:11,15,21). "These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season," and the psalmist ends, "I will sing unto the LORD as long as I live" (Psalm 104:27,33).
Psalms 104.whereWeAre: Psalm 103 praised God's mercy toward his people. Psalm 104 widens that praise to all creation, picturing God who "stretchest out the heavens like a curtain," sends springs for the wild donkeys, and gives even the young lions their food "from God" (Psalm 104:2,11,21). Psalm 105 turns from creation to Israel's own history, beginning with the covenant to Abraham.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Clothed with honour and majesty, provides food, water, and shelter for every creature in due season (Psalm 104:1,21,27).

keyThemes.explanation: Springs, trees, and creatures depend on each other and on God's provision.
Even the young lions seek their food from God, who provides for all in due season.
The psalmist marvels at God's wisdom in creation and resolves to keep singing praise.

explainedReferences.explanation: Making angels spirits and ministers a flame of fire.

Psalms 105.summary: "O give thanks unto the LORD... remember his marvellous works," for he "hath remembered his covenant for ever," sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Psalm 105:1,5,8-10). He sent Joseph ahead into Egypt, "whose feet they hurt with fetters," until "the king sent and loosed him" and "made him lord of his house" (Psalm 105:17-18,20-21). He sent Moses and Aaron with signs and plagues, then "brought forth his people with joy," giving them the lands of the heathen, "that they might observe his statutes, and keep his laws" (Psalm 105:37,43-45).
Psalms 105.whereWeAre: Psalm 104 praised God's care over creation. Psalm 105 turns to history, retelling the covenant God "remembered" with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Joseph's rise from prison to ruler in Egypt, and the plagues and exodus that followed (Psalm 105:8-10,17-22,27-36). Psalm 106 answers with the same history told as confession rather than praise.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, raised up Joseph, sent Moses and Aaron, and brought his people out of Egypt with joy (Psalm 105:8-10,26,43).

keyFigures.name: Joseph
keyFigures.role: Sold as a servant and imprisoned in fetters until the king freed him and made him ruler over his house (Psalm 105:17-18,20-21).

keyThemes.explanation: God remembered his covenant oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for a thousand generations.
Joseph's imprisonment in fetters became the path God used to save his family.
God brought his people out with joy so that they would keep his statutes.

Psalms 106.summary: Israel confesses, "We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly," recalling how their fathers "provoked him at the sea" yet God "saved them for his name's sake" (Psalm 106:6-8). In the wilderness they "made a calf in Horeb," and later in Canaan "sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils," so God "gave them into the hand of the heathen" (Psalm 106:19,37,41). Still, "many times did he deliver them," for "he remembered for them his covenant," and the psalm ends, "Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the heathen... Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting" (Psalm 106:43,45,47-48).
Psalms 106.whereWeAre: Psalm 105 told Israel's history as praise. Psalm 106 retells the same story as confession: "We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity," from the Red Sea to the golden calf to child sacrifice in Canaan (Psalm 106:6,19,37-38). It ends Book Four asking God to "gather us from among the heathen" (Psalm 106:47). Book Five opens with Psalm 107's matching call, "O give thanks unto the LORD, for he is good."

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Saved Israel at the Red Sea for his own name's sake and kept delivering them despite their repeated rebellion (Psalm 106:8,43,45).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Confesses generations of sin, from the golden calf to child sacrifice in Canaan, while pleading for God to gather them home (Psalm 106:6,19,37,47).

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Stands in the breach to turn away God's wrath after the golden calf, sparing the people from destruction (Psalm 106:23).

keyThemes.explanation: Israel confesses sinning just as their fathers did in Egypt and at the Red Sea.
Despite repeated rebellion, God kept delivering his people and remembered his covenant.
The psalm ends praying for God to gather his scattered people from among the nations.

Psalms 107.summary: The redeemed are called to give thanks because the LORD has redeemed them "from the hand of the enemy" and gathered them from every direction (Psalm 107:2-3). Four pictures of rescue follow: travelers lost in desert wandering, prisoners "bound in affliction and iron," the sick who draw near the gates of death, and sailors who "reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man" in a storm, each crying to the LORD and being delivered (Psalm 107:4,10,18,27). The psalm closes by turning rivers into wilderness and wilderness into water, bringing down princes and lifting up the poor, so that the wise "shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD" (Psalm 107:33-35,40-43).
Psalms 107.whereWeAre: Book Four ended with Psalm 106 confessing Israel's sin and asking God to "gather us from among the heathen" (Psalm 106:47). Psalm 107 opens Book Five by answering that prayer: the redeemed are called to give thanks because God has in fact gathered them "out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south" (Psalm 107:2-3). The four pictures of rescue that follow set the pattern for the thanksgiving psalms that fill the rest of the book, including Psalm 108's own call to give thanks among the nations.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Redeems and gathers his people from every direction, then rescues desert travelers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors who cry out to him (Psalm 107:2-3,6,13,19,28).

keyThemes.explanation: Desert wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and storm-tossed sailors each picture a different kind of trouble.
Each group cries to the LORD in trouble and is delivered, then is called to give thanks.
The wise who observe how God humbles the proud and lifts the needy will understand his lovingkindness.

Psalms 108.summary: David resolves to "awake early" and praise the LORD "among the nations," because God's mercy "is great above the heavens" (Psalm 108:2-4). He recalls God's promise to divide up Shechem, Gilead, and Moab, and asks who will bring him into Edom's "strong city" (Psalm 108:7-10). The psalm ends asking for help because "vain is the help of man," trusting that "through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies" (Psalm 108:12-13).
Psalms 108.whereWeAre: Psalm 107 called the redeemed to give thanks for rescue. Psalm 108 joins two earlier psalms of David, Psalm 57:7-11 and Psalm 60:5-12, into one song that moves from confident praise to a prayer for help in battle, saying "through God we shall do valiantly" (Psalm 108:13). Psalm 109 continues David's prayers under attack, turning from a hoped-for military victory to a plea against a specific, merciless accuser.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Resolves to praise God among the nations and prays for victory over Edom.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises territory to Israel by his own word and is asked to grant victory because human help is vain (Psalm 108:7-9,12-13).

keyThemes.explanation: David's heart is "fixed" to sing and give praise with his whole being.
The psalm asks for victory over Edom because vain is the help of man.
Only through God, not human strength, will Israel do valiantly and tread down its enemies.

Psalms 109.summary: David complains that "the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful" have attacked him with lying words, repaying his love with hatred (Psalm 109:2,5). He asks that the accuser's days be few and that "another take his office," a verse Peter later applies to Judas (Psalm 109:8; Acts 1:20). Because he is "poor and needy," he appeals to the LORD's mercy and vows, "I will greatly praise the LORD with my mouth" (Psalm 109:22,30).
Psalms 109.whereWeAre: Psalm 108 prayed for victory in battle. Psalm 109 turns to a more personal attack: David is surrounded by "words of hatred" from a lying accuser who repays his love with evil, and he asks God to judge that accuser's household (Psalm 109:3,5,8). Peter later applies verse 8 to Judas, "his bishoprick let another take" (Acts 1:20). Psalm 110 answers with an oracle of a very different king, enthroned at God's own right hand.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Pours out accusations against a merciless enemy and pleads for help according to God's steadfast love.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is asked to stand at the right hand of the poor and save David from those who condemn him (Psalm 109:26,31).

keyThemes.explanation: The accuser attacks with a lying tongue and words of hatred despite David's love.
David asks God to judge the accuser's household and cut off his memory.
Because he is poor and needy, David appeals to God's steadfast mercy rather than his own merit.

explainedReferences.explanation: Instruction that another take the person's office.

Psalms 110.summary: The LORD invites David's Lord to "sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool," a verse Jesus later quotes about himself (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 22:44). God sends this ruler's rod of strength out of Zion and swears, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek," which Hebrews applies to Christ's priesthood (Psalm 110:2,4; Hebrews 5:6). He will strike through kings and judge among the nations before lifting up his head (Psalm 110:5-7).
Psalms 110.whereWeAre: Psalm 109 pleaded for vindication against a merciless accuser. Psalm 110 answers with a royal oracle: "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool" (Psalm 110:1), a verse Jesus quotes to ask how David's own son could be David's Lord (Matthew 22:43-44) and Hebrews uses to describe Christ's eternal priesthood "after the order of Melchizedek" (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 5:6). Psalm 111 follows with an acrostic hymn praising the works of that same LORD.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Jesus points to this psalm to ask how David could call his own son "Lord" (Matthew 22:43-44).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Enthrones the king at his right hand and swears him an eternal priesthood after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:1,4).

keyThemes.explanation: The enthroned ruler is seated at God's right hand and sent to rule from Zion.
God's oath makes the ruler a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
God himself strikes through kings and judges the nations on the ruler's behalf.

explainedReferences.explanation: About sitting at God's right hand.
Same event: These passages explicitly quote David's statement about sitting at the Lord's right hand.
Same event: These passages explicitly quote David's statement about sitting at the Lord's right hand.
Same event: These passages explicitly quote David's statement about sitting at the Lord's right hand.
David's words about the Lord speaking to his Lord.
The appointment of a priest forever after Melchizedek's order.
The declaration of a priest forever after Melchizedek's order.
The appointment of a priest forever after Melchizedek's order.

Psalms 111.summary: The worshiper resolves to "praise the LORD with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright" (Psalm 111:1). God's works are "great" and "honourable and glorious," and he "hath made his wonderful works to be remembered," giving food to those who fear him and remembering his covenant forever (Psalm 111:2-5). The psalm ends, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom... his praise endureth for ever" (Psalm 111:10).
Psalms 111.whereWeAre: Psalm 110 announced an enthroned priest-king at God's right hand. Psalm 111 steps back into communal praise, an acrostic hymn in which each short line begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, celebrating the LORD's works and covenant (Psalm 111:1). Psalm 112 is built the same way, pairing this praise of God with a portrait of the person who fears him.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Does great and wonderful works, keeps his covenant forever, and gives understanding to those who fear him (Psalm 111:2,5,10).

keyThemes.explanation: God's wonderful works are made to be remembered by his people.
God's commandments stand fast forever, done in truth and uprightness.
The fear of the LORD is called the beginning of wisdom.

Psalms 112.summary: "Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD": his descendants will be mighty, and "wealth and riches shall be in his house" (Psalm 112:1-3). He is gracious, lends freely, and guides his affairs with discretion, so that "his horn shall be exalted with honour," a line Paul later echoes about generosity (Psalm 112:5,9; 2 Corinthians 9:9). Because his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD, he will not be afraid, while "the desire of the wicked shall perish" (Psalm 112:7-8,10).
Psalms 112.whereWeAre: Psalm 111 praised the LORD's own works in an acrostic hymn. Psalm 112 is a matching acrostic that turns to the person who fears him, promising that his "righteousness endureth for ever" just as God's does (Psalm 112:3; compare Psalm 111:3). Psalm 113 then widens the call to praise from this one blessed man to all the LORD's servants everywhere.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is feared by the blessed man whose house the psalm describes, though named only in the opening acrostic line (Psalm 112:1).

keyThemes.explanation: The blessed man greatly delights in the LORD's commandments.
He disperses freely and gives to the poor, and his righteousness endures forever.
His heart is fixed and unafraid, trusting in the LORD even in bad news.

explainedReferences.explanation: Description of generosity to the poor and enduring righteousness.

Psalms 113.summary: "Servants of the LORD" are called to praise his name "from the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same" (Psalm 113:1,3). Though he "dwelleth on high," he "humbleth himself to behold" heaven and earth, raising "the poor out of the dust" and lifting "the needy out of the dunghill" to sit with princes (Psalm 113:5-8). He also "maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children" (Psalm 113:9).
Psalms 113.whereWeAre: Psalm 112 pictured one blessed man who fears the LORD. Psalm 113 widens the call to praise to "ye servants of the LORD" everywhere, opening the Hallel psalms (113-118) that Jewish tradition sings at Passover (Psalm 113:1). It praises God for lifting the poor "out of the dust" and giving the barren woman a home, themes Psalm 114 continues by recalling how the same God once lifted Israel out of Egypt.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is exalted above all nations yet humbles himself to lift the poor from the dust and give the barren woman a home (Psalm 113:4-9).

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD is high above all nations, with his glory above the heavens.
God humbles himself to raise the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap.
The poor are seated with princes and the barren woman becomes a joyful mother.

Psalms 114.summary: "When Israel went out of Egypt," the sea "saw it, and fled," and Jordan "was driven back" (Psalm 114:1,3). Mountains "skipped like rams," trembling at "the presence of the God of Jacob" (Psalm 114:4,7). That same God "turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters" (Psalm 114:8).
Psalms 114.whereWeAre: Psalm 113 praised God for lifting up the lowly. Psalm 114 looks back to the greatest such reversal, "when Israel went out of Egypt," picturing the sea fleeing and the Jordan driven back, mountains skipping "like rams" before "the God of Jacob" (Psalm 114:1,3-4,7). Psalm 115 follows by turning from God's power in history to his superiority over the lifeless idols of the nations.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Leads Israel out of Egypt, making sea and river flee and turning rock into flowing water (Psalm 114:1,3,8).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalm recalls Israel's departure from Egypt, a people of strange language.
Sea, river, mountains, and hills are pictured fleeing and trembling before God.
The earth is told to tremble at the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob.

Psalms 115.summary: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory," because the nations' idols "have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not" (Psalm 115:1,5). Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the LORD are each called to "trust thou in the LORD: he is their help and their shield" (Psalm 115:9-11). The psalm ends, "The dead praise not the LORD... But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and for evermore" (Psalm 115:17-18).
Psalms 115.whereWeAre: Psalm 114 recalled God's power at the exodus. Psalm 115 contrasts that living power with the idols of the nations, which "have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not" (Psalm 115:5). It asks glory for God's name alone and calls Israel, "the house of Aaron," and all who fear the LORD to trust him, a trust Psalm 116 pictures in one rescued worshiper's own thanksgiving (Psalm 115:9-11).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is contrasted with lifeless idols and called the help and shield of Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear him (Psalm 115:4-5,9-11).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalm asks that glory go to God's name, not to Israel itself.
Idols of silver and gold have mouths, eyes, and ears that cannot work.
The LORD blesses those who fear him, both small and great.

Psalms 116.summary: "I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice," the worshiper says, recalling how "the sorrows of death compassed me" before the LORD delivered his soul (Psalm 116:1,3,8). Having been preserved, he asks, "What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?" and answers by taking "the cup of salvation" and calling on God's name (Psalm 116:12-13). He vows twice to "pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people," in the courts of the LORD's house in Jerusalem (Psalm 116:14,18-19).
Psalms 116.whereWeAre: Psalm 115 called Israel to trust the living God rather than lifeless idols. Psalm 116 shows that trust fulfilled in one worshiper rescued from death, who vows thanksgiving "in the presence of all his people" (Psalm 116:14). Psalm 117 then takes up that same call to praise and sends it out to "all ye nations."

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hears the worshiper's voice, delivers his soul from death, and deals bountifully with him (Psalm 116:1,6,8).

keyThemes.explanation: The worshiper loves the LORD because he heard his cry and saved him from death.
He vows to pay his vows and offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving before all God's people.
Having been loosed from his bonds, he calls himself the LORD's servant.

explainedReferences.explanation: Believing and therefore speaking.

Psalms 117.summary: "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people," a call Paul later quotes to show that Gentiles are meant to glorify God (Psalm 117:1; Romans 15:11). The reason is given in a single line: "his merciful kindness is great toward us: and the truth of the LORD endureth for ever" (Psalm 117:2).
Psalms 117.whereWeAre: Psalm 116 was one worshiper's personal thanksgiving. Psalm 117, the shortest psalm and shortest chapter in the Bible at two verses, widens that praise to "all ye nations," a line Paul later quotes to show that Gentiles too praise God (Psalm 117:1; Romans 15:11). Psalm 118 then closes the Hallel with a longer thanksgiving for deliverance.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is praised by all nations for his great merciful kindness and enduring truth (Psalm 117:1-2).

keyThemes.explanation: All nations and all people are called to praise the LORD.
God's merciful kindness toward his people is described as great.
The truth of the LORD is said to endure for ever.

explainedReferences.explanation: The command for all nations and peoples to praise the Lord.

Psalms 118.summary: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever," Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the LORD are each told to say (Psalm 118:1-4). Having called on the LORD "in distress" and found him on his side, the worshiper declares, "The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner," words Jesus applies to himself (Psalm 118:5,22; Matthew 21:42). The crowds at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem later shout its blessing, "Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD," and open the gates of righteousness to enter and give thanks (Psalm 118:19-20,26; Matthew 21:9).
Psalms 118.whereWeAre: Psalm 117 called all nations to praise. Psalm 118 closes the Hallel with a longer thanksgiving for deliverance: the crowds later shout its blessing on "he that cometh in the name of the LORD" when Jesus enters Jerusalem, and Jesus applies its "stone which the builders refused" to himself (Psalm 118:22,26; Matthew 21:9,42). Psalm 119 follows with the longest psalm in the Bible, an extended meditation on that same LORD's law.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Answers the worshiper's cry in distress and becomes his strength, song, and salvation (Psalm 118:5,14).

keyThemes.explanation: The worshiper gives thanks because the LORD answered him and became his salvation.
The stone the builders refused becomes the head stone of the corner, a verse the New Testament applies to Jesus.
Worshipers are called through the gates of righteousness into public thanksgiving.

explainedReferences.explanation: The confession that the Lord is one's helper and there is no reason to fear.
The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is directly quoted.
The image of the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone.
The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is directly quoted.
The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is directly quoted.
The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone.
The crowd quotes the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
The declaration blessing the one who comes in the Lord's name is repeated.
The declaration blessing the one who comes in the Lord's name is repeated.
The crowds shout the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
The declaration blessing the one who comes in the Lord's name is repeated.

Psalms 119.summary: Across twenty-two alphabetic stanzas the psalmist calls God's word "a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" and declares, "O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day" (Psalm 119:105,97). He admits affliction has taught him obedience, "Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word," and compares himself to "a bottle in the smoke" that still does not forget God's statutes (Psalm 119:67,83). The psalm ends still searching: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant; for I do not forget thy commandments" (Psalm 119:176).
Psalms 119.whereWeAre: Psalm 118 closed the Hallel with thanksgiving for rescue. Psalm 119 is the longest psalm and longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses in twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, meditating at length on the LORD's law, word, and judgments (Psalm 119:105). Psalm 120 then opens the fifteen psalms titled A Song of degrees (120-134), shifting from this long meditation to short pilgrim songs sung on the road to Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is the giver of the law, word, and judgments that the entire psalm meditates on and clings to (Psalm 119:105,97).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalmist calls God's law his delight and meditates on it all day.
Affliction is described as good because it taught obedience and kept him from straying.
Repeated prayers ask God to teach statutes and incline the heart toward his testimonies.

Psalms 120.summary: "In my distress I cried unto the LORD, and he heard me," the pilgrim begins, asking deliverance "from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue" (Psalm 120:1-2). He pictures that tongue punished with "sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper" (Psalm 120:4). Grieving that he dwells among those who hate peace, he says, "I am for peace: but when I speak, they are for war" (Psalm 120:5-7).
Psalms 120.whereWeAre: Psalm 119 was a long, settled meditation on God's law. Psalm 120 opens a shorter and more restless set of fifteen psalms titled "A Song of degrees" (120-134), traditionally sung by pilgrims climbing the road to Jerusalem for the feasts. Its first pilgrim cries out against lying lips and longs for peace among people who "are for war" (Psalm 120:7), a longing Psalm 121 answers by looking to the LORD as a keeper for the journey itself.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hears the pilgrim's cry in distress against lying lips and a deceitful tongue (Psalm 120:1-2).

keyThemes.explanation: The pilgrim asks rescue from lying lips and a deceitful tongue.
He grieves living among people in Mesech and Kedar who hate peace.
He describes himself as a man of peace surrounded by those who want war.

Psalms 121.summary: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help," the pilgrim says, finding that help in "the LORD, which made heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:1-2). That keeper "shall neither slumber nor sleep," shading the traveler so that "the sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night" (Psalm 121:4,6). The psalm closes, "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore" (Psalm 121:8).
Psalms 121.whereWeAre: Psalm 120 cried out in distress at the start of the pilgrim road. Psalm 121 answers with confidence, lifting its eyes "unto the hills" and trusting the maker of heaven and earth as a keeper who "shall neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:1,4). Psalm 122 continues the journey, picturing the pilgrim's feet finally standing within Jerusalem's gates.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Made heaven and earth and keeps the pilgrim from all evil, neither slumbering nor sleeping (Psalm 121:2-4,7-8).

keyThemes.explanation: The pilgrim's help comes not from the hills themselves but from their maker.
The LORD is called Israel's keeper, who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
God preserves the traveler from sun, moon, and all evil, going out and coming in.

Psalms 122.summary: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD," the pilgrim recalls, and now "our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem" (Psalm 122:1-2). The tribes go up there together, and the "thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David" are set in the city (Psalm 122:4-5). He closes, "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem... Peace be within thy walls, and prosperity within thy palaces" (Psalm 122:6-7).
Psalms 122.whereWeAre: Psalm 121 trusted the LORD as a keeper for the road. Psalm 122 arrives at the destination: "Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem," where the tribes gather and David's thrones of judgment stand (Psalm 122:2,4-5). It prays for the city's peace, a peace Psalm 123 then asks for amid the pilgrims' own scorn and hardship.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Traditional attribution in the superscription. Jerusalem is named as the seat of his dynasty's thrones of judgment (Psalm 122:5).

keyThemes.explanation: The pilgrim rejoices at the invitation to go up to the house of the LORD.
The tribes of the LORD go up together to give thanks at Jerusalem.
The psalm prays for peace and prosperity within the city's walls.

Psalms 123.summary: "Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens," the pilgrims pray, watching for mercy "as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters" (Psalm 123:1-2). They ask mercy because they "are exceedingly filled with contempt" from the proud and those at ease (Psalm 123:3-4).
Psalms 123.whereWeAre: Psalm 122 celebrated arrival at Jerusalem. Psalm 123 turns from that joy to the hardship pilgrims still faced, lifting its eyes to God "that dwellest in the heavens" while "filled with the scorning of those that are at ease" (Psalm 123:1,4). Psalm 124 answers by looking back at how often the LORD has already rescued Israel from such hostility.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is asked for mercy by pilgrims enduring scorn from the secure and the proud (Psalm 123:1-3).

keyThemes.explanation: The pilgrims watch the LORD as a servant watches a master's hand.
They twice ask the LORD directly to have mercy upon them.
The pilgrims describe themselves as filled with contempt from the proud.

Psalms 124.summary: "If it had not been the LORD who was on our side," Israel confesses, "now may Israel say," its enemies would have swallowed it up alive and its soul would have been overwhelmed like a flood (Psalm 124:1-4). Instead, "Blessed be the LORD, who hath not given us as a prey to their teeth" (Psalm 124:6). The psalm ends, "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped" (Psalm 124:7).
Psalms 124.whereWeAre: Psalm 123 asked for mercy amid contempt. Psalm 124 answers by recalling Israel's history of rescue, saying that without the LORD "on our side" the nation would have been swallowed alive (Psalm 124:1-3). Psalm 125 then compares that same trust to Mount Zion, which "cannot be removed, but abideth for ever" (Psalm 125:1).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Declares that without the LORD on its side it would have been overwhelmed by its enemies (Psalm 124:1-5).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Did not give Israel as prey and broke the snare so it could escape (Psalm 124:6-8).

keyThemes.explanation: Without the LORD, Israel's enemies would have swallowed it up alive.
Israel's soul escapes like a bird when the fowler's snare is broken.
Israel's help is said to be in the name of the LORD, maker of heaven and earth.

Psalms 125.summary: "They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed, but abideth for ever," just as mountains stand around Jerusalem (Psalm 125:1-2). The psalm asks the LORD to "do good" to the upright but promises that "the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous," lest they too turn to iniquity (Psalm 125:3-4). It closes asking peace upon Israel (Psalm 125:5).
Psalms 125.whereWeAre: Psalm 124 thanked the LORD for past rescue. Psalm 125 turns that trust into a steady image: those who trust in the LORD are "as mount Zion, which cannot be removed, but abideth for ever," just as mountains surround Jerusalem itself (Psalm 125:1-2). Psalm 126 then recalls one specific time that trust was rewarded, when the LORD "turned again the captivity of Zion" (Psalm 126:1).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Surrounds his people as the mountains surround Jerusalem and is asked to do good to the upright (Psalm 125:2-4).

keyThemes.explanation: Those who trust in the LORD are compared to the immovable Mount Zion.
The rod of the wicked will not remain over the land of the righteous.
The psalm closes by asking peace specifically upon Israel.

Psalms 126.summary: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream," the people recall, their mouths "filled with laughter" so that even the nations said, "The LORD hath done great things for them" (Psalm 126:1-2). They now ask, "Turn again our captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south," trusting that "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:4-5). The psalm ends picturing one who goes out weeping with seed but "shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him" (Psalm 126:6).
Psalms 126.whereWeAre: Psalm 125 pictured Israel as unmovable as Zion. Psalm 126 recalls a specific fulfillment of that security, when "the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion" and the people "were like them that dream," their mouths "filled with laughter" (Psalm 126:1-2), likely the return from Babylon after 538 BC. It ends asking for a future harvest of joy, which Psalm 127 answers by insisting that such building and increase come from the LORD alone.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Turned again the captivity of Zion and is asked to do so again, like streams returning to the dry south (Psalm 126:1,4).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Remembers laughing like those who dream after the LORD's great deliverance (Psalm 126:1-2).

keyThemes.explanation: The returning people are compared to those who dream, filled with laughter.
The psalm asks the LORD to restore fortunes further, like streams in the dry south.
Sowing in tears is promised a harvest of joy and returning with sheaves.

Psalms 127.summary: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain" (Psalm 127:1). It is vain to rise early and sit up late, "for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2). Children, by contrast, are "an heritage of the LORD," like arrows in a warrior's hand, and the man whose quiver is full of them "shall not be ashamed" (Psalm 127:3-5).
Psalms 127.whereWeAre: Psalm 126 prayed for a harvest after tears. Psalm 127, titled for Solomon, insists that such labor is futile without the LORD: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it" (Psalm 127:1). It calls children "an heritage of the LORD" rather than mere human achievement (Psalm 127:3), a household blessing Psalm 128 extends to the whole family of the one who fears the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Named in the title. The psalm's wisdom sayings about building, watching, and children fit the wisdom literature associated with him.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Builds the house and keeps the city; without him labor is vain and sleep itself is his gift (Psalm 127:1-2).

keyThemes.explanation: Building a house or keeping a city in one's own strength is called vain without the LORD.
Sleep itself is described as something the LORD gives his beloved.
Children are called an heritage of the LORD, like arrows in a warrior's hand.

Psalms 128.summary: "Blessed is every one that feareth the LORD; that walketh in his ways," who will eat the labor of his own hands and prosper (Psalm 128:1-2). His wife will be "as a fruitful vine," his children "like olive plants round about thy table" (Psalm 128:3). The psalm closes praying that he see "the good of Jerusalem all the days of thy life" and live to see "thy children's children, and peace upon Israel" (Psalm 128:5-6).
Psalms 128.whereWeAre: Psalm 127 called children a heritage from the LORD. Psalm 128 widens that household blessing to everyone who fears the LORD, promising a fruitful wife, children "like olive plants," and the chance to see "thy children's children" (Psalm 128:3,6). Psalm 129 then turns from one household's peace to the whole nation's long history of surviving affliction.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Blesses the household of the one who fears him with fruitful labor, family, and long life (Psalm 128:1,4-5).

keyThemes.explanation: The one who fears the LORD eats the labor of his own hands.
His wife and children are pictured as a fruitful vine and olive plants.
The blessing extends outward to seeing the good of Jerusalem and peace upon Israel.

Psalms 129.summary: "Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth," Israel says, "yet they have not prevailed against me," though "the plowers plowed upon my back" (Psalm 129:1-3). "The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked" (Psalm 129:4). The psalm ends wishing those who hate Zion to wither like "grass upon the housetops," never reaped or blessed (Psalm 129:5-8).
Psalms 129.whereWeAre: Psalm 128 blessed one household that fears the LORD. Psalm 129 speaks for the whole nation, recalling affliction "from my youth" yet declaring that enemies "have not prevailed" against it (Psalm 129:1-2). Psalm 130 follows with an individual's matching cry, "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD" (Psalm 130:1).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Recalls being afflicted from its youth yet declares that its enemies have not prevailed (Psalm 129:1-2).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is called righteous for cutting asunder the cords of the wicked (Psalm 129:4).

keyThemes.explanation: Israel has been afflicted from its youth but was not overcome.
The LORD's righteousness is credited with cutting the cords of the wicked.
The psalm asks that those who hate Zion wither like rootless grass.

Psalms 130.summary: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD," the worshiper begins, asking that God's ears be attentive (Psalm 130:1-2). He knows that if the LORD marked iniquities no one could stand, "but there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared" (Psalm 130:3-4). He waits for the LORD "more than they that watch for the morning," and tells Israel to hope in him, "for with the LORD there is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption" (Psalm 130:6-7).
Psalms 130.whereWeAre: Psalm 129 spoke for the whole nation's endurance. Psalm 130 narrows to one voice crying "out of the depths," trusting in forgiveness and waiting for the LORD "more than they that watch for the morning" (Psalm 130:1,6). Psalm 131, by contrast, pictures a soul already quieted, like a weaned child who no longer cries out at all.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Offers forgiveness and plenteous redemption to the one who cries from the depths (Psalm 130:4,7).

keyThemes.explanation: The worshiper cries to the LORD out of the depths of his trouble.
Forgiveness, not strict judgment of iniquity, is what makes God feared.
The worshiper waits for the LORD more than watchmen wait for morning.

Psalms 131.summary: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty," David says, "neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me" (Psalm 131:1). Instead he has "behaved and quieted" himself, his soul "even as a weaned child" (Psalm 131:2). He closes, "Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever" (Psalm 131:3).
Psalms 131.whereWeAre: Psalm 130 waited anxiously for the LORD. Psalm 131 answers with quiet contentment, David comparing his soul to "a weaned child" who no longer demands anything, and telling Israel to "hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever" (Psalm 131:2-3). Psalm 132 then recalls a very different, restless vow David once made, to find the LORD a dwelling place.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Rejects proud ambition and compares his quieted soul to a weaned child.

keyThemes.explanation: David declares his heart not haughty and his eyes not lofty.
His soul is compared to a weaned child, quieted rather than demanding.
The psalm ends calling all Israel to hope in the LORD forever.

Psalms 132.summary: The psalm recalls how David swore he would not rest "until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob" (Psalm 132:2,5). In answer, "the LORD hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne," so long as his children keep God's covenant (Psalm 132:11-12). "For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation," promising to clothe its priests with salvation and make David's horn "to bud" there (Psalm 132:13,16-17).
Psalms 132.whereWeAre: Psalm 131 pictured a quieted soul content with little.
