Psalm 132 recalls David's restless vow not to rest "until I find out a place for the LORD" and God's answering promise that his line would sit on the throne and that the LORD had "desired" Zion "for his habitation" (Psalm 132:5,13); Solomon later quotes this psalm's words at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 6:41-42). Psalm 133 follows with a short song praising the unity Zion's worship was meant to create.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Swore not to rest until he found a dwelling place for the LORD, an oath Solomon later quotes at the temple's dedication (Psalm 132:2-5; 2 Chronicles 6:41-42).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Swears in return that David's line will sit on the throne and that he has chosen Zion for his dwelling (Psalm 132:11,13).

keyThemes.explanation: David vows restlessness until he secures a dwelling place for the LORD.
God swears that David's own offspring will sit upon his throne.
The LORD declares he has chosen and desired Zion for his resting place forever.

Psalms 133.summary: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" the psalm begins (Psalm 133:1). That unity is compared to "the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard," and to "the dew of Hermon" falling on the mountains of Zion (Psalm 133:2-3). "For there the LORD commanded the blessing, even life for evermore" (Psalm 133:3).
Psalms 133.whereWeAre: Psalm 132 celebrated the LORD choosing Zion as his dwelling. Psalm 133 praises the unity that worship there was meant to create among David's people, comparing it to precious oil running down Aaron's beard and dew falling on the mountains of Zion, "for there the LORD commanded the blessing, even life for evermore" (Psalm 133:2-3). Psalm 134 closes the songs of degrees with a blessing for the Levites who kept watch there through the night.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Traditional attribution in the superscription. The psalm he is credited with celebrates brothers dwelling together in unity.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Commands the blessing of life for evermore at Zion, where this unity is pictured gathering (Psalm 133:3).

keyThemes.explanation: Brothers dwelling together in unity are called good and pleasant.
Unity is compared to anointing oil running down Aaron's beard and garments.
The LORD commands the blessing of life for evermore at the place of unity.

Psalms 134.summary: "Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD," the pilgrims call to the Levites on duty (Psalm 134:1). They are told to "lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD" (Psalm 134:2). The psalm answers with a blessing back: "The LORD that made heaven and earth bless thee out of Zion" (Psalm 134:3).
Psalms 134.whereWeAre: Psalm 133 praised brothers dwelling together in unity. Psalm 134 closes the fifteen songs of degrees with a short exchange between pilgrims and the Levites who "by night stand in the house of the LORD," calling them to bless him and receive his blessing in return (Psalm 134:1-3). Psalm 135 then opens a fresh set of praise psalms by calling those same servants of the LORD to praise him for his works in history.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is blessed by the night-watching Levites and in turn blesses them out of Zion (Psalm 134:1-3).

keyThemes.explanation: Levites who stand by night in the LORD's house are called to bless him.
The pilgrims' call to bless God is answered with a blessing from Zion.
The one who blesses out of Zion is identified as the maker of heaven and earth.

Psalms 135.summary: "Praise ye the LORD... Ye that stand in the house of the LORD," are called to praise him, "for the LORD is good: sing praises unto his name; for it is pleasant" (Psalm 135:1-3). He smote Egypt's firstborn, brought Israel out, and defeated "Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan," giving their land to Israel as an heritage (Psalm 135:8-12). By contrast, "the idols of the heathen are silver and gold, the work of men's hands," with mouths that cannot speak (Psalm 135:15-16).
Psalms 135.whereWeAre: Psalm 134 closed the songs of degrees with a blessing exchanged in the temple at night. Psalm 135 opens a new set of praise psalms, again calling the LORD's servants "that stand in the house of the LORD" to praise him, now for his power over idols and his acts in Egypt, the wilderness, and Canaan (Psalm 135:2,8-11). Psalm 136 answers with a full recitation of that same history, repeating "for his mercy endureth for ever" after every line.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Has chosen Israel for his own treasure and defeated Egypt and the kings Sihon and Og on its behalf (Psalm 135:4,8-11).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalm recalls God smiting Egypt's firstborn and defeating Sihon and Og.
Idols of silver and gold are contrasted with the LORD who does whatever he pleases.
Israel, the house of Aaron, and the house of Levi are each called to bless the LORD.

Psalms 136.summary: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever," repeated after every line (Psalm 136:1). That mercy is traced through creation, "to him that by wisdom made the heavens," and through the exodus, "to him which divided the Red sea into parts" and "overthrew Pharaoh and his host" (Psalm 136:5,13,15). It continues through the defeat of "Sihon king of the Amorites... Og the king of Bashan," down to God's present care, "who giveth food to all flesh" (Psalm 136:19-20,25).
Psalms 136.whereWeAre: Psalm 135 praised the LORD for creation and for defeating Sihon and Og. Psalm 136, called the Great Hallel in Jewish tradition, retells that same history at length, with a leader singing each line and the people answering "for his mercy endureth for ever" after every one of its twenty-six verses (Psalm 136:1). Psalm 137 answers with a very different memory, the grief of exiles who no longer have a temple to sing in at all.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is thanked in every verse for his enduring mercy shown in creation, the exodus, and ongoing provision (Psalm 136:1,5,13,25).

keyThemes.explanation: God's mercy is traced from making the heavens and earth to redeeming Israel.
The psalm credits God with giving food to all flesh.
Every one of the psalm's twenty-six verses ends with the same refrain of enduring mercy.

Psalms 137.summary: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion," hanging their harps on the willows (Psalm 137:1-2). Asked for "the songs of Zion," they ask, "How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?" and vow, "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning" (Psalm 137:3-5). The psalm ends with a fierce curse on Babylon and Edom, who cheered Jerusalem's fall and said, "Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof" (Psalm 137:7-9).
Psalms 137.whereWeAre: Psalm 136 recited Israel's history as unbroken praise. Psalm 137 answers from the other side of that history, exiles sitting "by the rivers of Babylon" who "wept, when we remembered Zion" and refuse to sing the LORD's song for their captors (Psalm 137:1,4). Psalm 138 returns to David's own voice giving thanks, a contrast the editors of this closing section seem to have placed deliberately.

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: The exiles weep by Babylon's rivers, refuse to sing for their captors, and vow never to forget Jerusalem (Psalm 137:1-6).

keyThemes.explanation: The exiles weep remembering Zion and hang their harps on the willows.
The exiles vow to prefer Jerusalem above their chief joy rather than forget it.
The psalm ends asking judgment on Edom and Babylon for Jerusalem's destruction.

Psalms 138.summary: "I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee," David says, because "in the day when I cried thou answeredst me" (Psalm 138:1,3). He foresees that "all the kings of the earth shall praise thee, O LORD, when they hear the words of thy mouth," for though the LORD is high, "yet hath he respect unto the lowly" (Psalm 138:4,6). The psalm ends in confidence: "The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever" (Psalm 138:8).
Psalms 138.whereWeAre: Psalm 137 voiced the exiles' grief and anger. Psalm 138 returns to David's thanksgiving, praising God "before the gods" for answering him and promising that even "all the kings of the earth" will one day praise the LORD (Psalm 138:1,4). Psalm 139 then turns from God's answers in time to his complete knowledge of the psalmist from before birth.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Gives thanks for God's answer and asks that his care continue.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Answers David's cry, respects the lowly, and will perfect what concerns him (Psalm 138:3,6,8).

keyThemes.explanation: David gives thanks with his whole heart because the LORD answered his cry.
Though the LORD is high, he has respect for the lowly while knowing the proud from afar.
David trusts the LORD to perfect what concerns him and not forsake his own work.

Psalms 139.summary: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me," David says, for God understands his thoughts "afar off" and is "acquainted with all my ways" (Psalm 139:1-3). He cannot flee that presence: "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there" (Psalm 139:8). He confesses, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made," for God "covered me in my mother's womb," and closes asking, "Search me, O God, and know my heart... and lead me in the way everlasting" (Psalm 139:13-14,23-24).
Psalms 139.whereWeAre: Psalm 138 trusted God to finish what he started. Psalm 139 explains why: the LORD has "searched me, and known me" completely, forming the psalmist in the womb and knowing his thoughts "afar off" (Psalm 139:1-2,13). It ends asking God to "search me" again and "lead me in the way everlasting," a self-examination Psalm 140 continues by asking protection from violent men who plot evil.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Praises the God who knows his every thought and formed him in the womb.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Searches and knows David completely, present in every place and forming him from before birth (Psalm 139:1-4,13).

keyThemes.explanation: God knows every thought and word before it is spoken.
David was formed and made in secret in his mother's womb.
The psalm ends asking God to search the heart and lead in the way everlasting.

Psalms 140.summary: "Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man," David prays, for "adders' poison is under their lips," a line Paul later quotes about human sinfulness (Psalm 140:1,3; Romans 3:13). He asks God to keep him from hidden snares and nets, trusting, "thou hast covered my head in the day of battle" (Psalm 140:4-5,7). He closes confident that "the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor" (Psalm 140:12).
Psalms 140.whereWeAre: Psalm 139 asked God to search the heart for any wicked way. Psalm 140 asks protection from a specific outward threat, violent men who "sharpened their tongues like a serpent" and spread nets and snares (Psalm 140:3,5). Psalm 141 continues the same concern turned inward, asking God to guard the psalmist's own mouth from evil speech.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Asks for safety from violent schemers and their traps.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is asked to preserve David from violent men and is trusted to maintain the cause of the afflicted (Psalm 140:1,12).

keyThemes.explanation: David asks to be kept from hidden snares, nets, and gins laid for him.
Violent men are pictured sharpening their tongues like serpents, with poison under their lips.
David trusts the LORD to maintain the cause of the afflicted and the right of the poor.

explainedReferences.explanation: The description of poison beneath deceitful lips.

Psalms 141.summary: "LORD, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me," David prays, asking that his prayer be "set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice" (Psalm 141:1-2). He asks, "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips," so that he will not be drawn into wicked works or eat the dainties of evildoers (Psalm 141:3-4). He closes asking to be kept "from the snares which they have laid for me," trusting, "in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute" (Psalm 141:8-9).
Psalms 141.whereWeAre: Psalm 140 asked protection from violent men's dangerous words. Psalm 141 turns that same concern inward, asking the LORD to "set a watch" before his own mouth so that his prayer rises "as incense" rather than becoming part of the evil he condemns (Psalm 141:2-3). Psalm 142 then narrows further to one specific, desperate moment, David's prayer from hiding in a cave.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Asks for guarded speech, acceptable prayer, and preservation from evildoers' snares.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is asked to watch over David's mouth and keep him from the snares of evildoers (Psalm 141:3,9).

keyThemes.explanation: David asks God to set a watch before his mouth and keep the door of his lips.
His prayer and lifted hands are compared to incense and the evening sacrifice.
He asks not to be inclined to evil or to eat the dainties of evildoers.

Psalms 142.summary: "I cried unto the LORD with my voice," David says, pouring out his complaint from the cave where he hid from Saul (Psalm 142:1-2; 1 Samuel 22:1). He looks and finds "no man that would know me: refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul" (Psalm 142:4). He cries, "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name: the righteous shall compass me about; for thou shalt deal bountifully with me" (Psalm 142:7).
Psalms 142.whereWeAre: Psalm 141 asked God to guard the psalmist's own mouth. Psalm 142 is titled "A Prayer when he was in the cave," the one time David hid from Saul in a cave (1 Samuel 22:1; 24:3), crying out that "no man cared for my soul" and asking God to "bring my soul out of prison" (Psalm 142:4,7). Psalm 143 continues David's prayers under pressure, now asking for guidance rather than simply rescue.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist, hiding in a cave from Saul. Pours out complaint and asks God to bring him out for thanksgiving.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is David's refuge and portion when no one else cares for his soul (Psalm 142:5).

keyThemes.explanation: David finds no man who cares for his soul and pours out his complaint to God alone.
David calls the LORD his refuge and his portion in the land of the living.
He asks to be brought out of prison-like trouble so he can praise God's name.

Psalms 143.summary: "Hear my prayer, O LORD... enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified," David prays, a line Paul later echoes (Psalm 143:1-2; Romans 3:20). Overwhelmed, he remembers "the days of old" and stretches out his hands, his soul thirsting "as a thirsty land" (Psalm 143:5-6). He asks, "Teach me to do thy will; for thou art my God," and closes asking rescue "for thy righteousness' sake," since "I am thy servant" (Psalm 143:10-12).
Psalms 143.whereWeAre: Psalm 142 cried out from isolation in the cave. Psalm 143 continues David's distress but asks for more than rescue: guidance and a right spirit, confessing that "in thy sight shall no man living be justified," a line Paul later echoes (Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:20). Psalm 144 answers with a shift back to confidence, praising God as the one who trains David's hands for battle.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Seeks swift help, recalls past deeds, and asks guidance because no one is righteous before God.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is asked to answer in faithfulness and righteousness and to lead David in the way of uprightness (Psalm 143:1,10).

keyThemes.explanation: David asks God not to enter into judgment, since no living person could be justified.
He asks to be taught God's will and led in the way of uprightness.
David meditates on the days of old and the work of God's hands.

Psalms 144.summary: "Blessed be the LORD my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight," David says, calling him his goodness, fortress, and deliverer (Psalm 144:1-2). He marvels, "LORD, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him!" since human life is "like to vanity" (Psalm 144:3-4). He prays for sons like "plants grown up," daughters like polished "corner stones," and full garners, concluding, "Happy is that people, whose God is the LORD" (Psalm 144:12-13,15).
Psalms 144.whereWeAre: Psalm 143 asked for guidance amid distress. Psalm 144 answers with renewed confidence, praising God as the one "which teacheth my hands to war," drawing on language from Psalm 18 and Psalm 8 (Psalm 144:1). It ends blessing a people whose sons, daughters, flocks, and fields all prosper, a flourishing Psalm 145 then turns into pure praise of God's greatness.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Praises God as his defender in battle and prays for his people's flourishing.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Teaches David's hands to war and is called his strength, fortress, and deliverer (Psalm 144:1-2).

keyThemes.explanation: David credits the LORD with teaching his hands for battle and delivering him from the sword.
He asks rescue from strange children whose words are false and promises a new song of praise.
The psalm prays for flourishing sons, daughters, flocks, and fields.

Psalms 145.summary: "I will extol thee, my God, O king," David says, "and I will bless thy name for ever and ever," since "his greatness is unsearchable" (Psalm 145:1,3). He declares the LORD "gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy," good to all and near to all who call on him in truth (Psalm 145:8,18). He ends, "The LORD preserveth all them that love him... My mouth shall speak the praise of the LORD" (Psalm 145:20-21).
Psalms 145.whereWeAre: Psalm 144 prayed for a flourishing, God-blessed people. Psalm 145, an acrostic moving through the Hebrew alphabet, turns that blessing into pure praise of God's own greatness, promising that "one generation shall praise thy works to another" (Psalm 145:4). Psalm 146 then opens the five closing "Hallelujah" psalms (146-150) that end the book.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Leads an alphabetic hymn celebrating God's greatness, compassion, and provision.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is gracious and full of compassion, upholds all who fall, and is near to all who call on him in truth (Psalm 145:8,14,18).

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD's greatness is called unsearchable, declared from one generation to another.
God is gracious and full of compassion, satisfying the desire of every living thing.
Each generation is called to praise God's works and declare his mighty acts.

Psalms 146.summary: "Praise ye the LORD... Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help," for "his breath goeth forth... in that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:1,3-4). Instead, happy is the one whose help is the God who made heaven and earth and "keepeth truth for ever," who executes judgment for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry (Psalm 146:5-7). "The LORD preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow," and "shall reign for ever" (Psalm 146:9-10).
Psalms 146.whereWeAre: Psalm 145 praised God's greatness across every generation. Psalm 146 opens the five psalms that close the book (146-150), each beginning and ending with "Praise ye the LORD," contrasting trust in "princes" who perish with trust in the God who "executeth judgment for the oppressed" (Psalm 146:3,7). Psalm 147 continues this closing praise by turning to God's care for Jerusalem and for creation together.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Made heaven and earth, keeps truth forever, and executes judgment for the oppressed, hungry, and vulnerable (Psalm 146:6-9).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalm warns against trusting in princes, whose plans perish with them.
The LORD preserves strangers and relieves the fatherless and widow.
The LORD is said to reign for ever, to all generations.

Psalms 147.summary: "The LORD doth build up Jerusalem: he gathereth together the outcasts of Israel," healing "the broken in heart" and binding up their wounds (Psalm 147:2-3). The same God "telleth the number of the stars" and "calleth them all by their names," yet also "giveth snow like wool" and "casteth forth his ice like morsels" (Psalm 147:4,16-17). He "sheweth his word unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Israel," dealing with no other nation this way (Psalm 147:19-20).
Psalms 147.whereWeAre: Psalm 146 contrasted perishing princes with the everlasting LORD. Psalm 147 joins that same LORD's care for the brokenhearted and the rebuilding of Jerusalem with his care over nature, naming the stars and sending snow and rain (Psalm 147:2-4,16). Psalm 148 then widens the call to praise outward from Jerusalem to all of creation at once.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Rebuilds Jerusalem, heals the brokenhearted, names every star, and governs the weather (Psalm 147:2-4,16-18).

keyThemes.explanation: God rebuilds Jerusalem and heals those who are brokenhearted.
He names the stars, sends rain, and feeds the beasts and young ravens.
God's word and statutes are given specifically to Jacob and Israel.

Psalms 148.summary: "Praise ye the LORD from the heavens... Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light," for "he commanded, and they were created" (Psalm 148:1,3,5). The call continues to earth, "ye dragons, and all deeps," fire and hail, mountains and cedars, beasts and creeping things, "kings of the earth, and all people" (Psalm 148:7,9,11). "Let them praise the name of the LORD: for his name alone is excellent; his glory is above the earth and heaven" (Psalm 148:13).
Psalms 148.whereWeAre: Psalm 147 joined God's care for Jerusalem with his care for nature. Psalm 148 widens the call to praise to everything at once, heavens and "dragons" of the deep, weather and mountains, "kings of the earth" and "children," all summoned to praise the LORD's "name alone" (Psalm 148:7,11-13). Psalm 149 then narrows back to Israel specifically, celebrating its maker with dancing and song.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is praised by the heavens and the earth together because he created them and his name alone is excellent (Psalm 148:5,13).

keyThemes.explanation: Heavens, sun, moon, stars, sea creatures, and weather are all called to praise.
Kings, princes, judges, young and old are all included in the call to praise.
The LORD's name alone is called excellent, his glory above earth and heaven.

Psalms 149.summary: "Sing unto the LORD a new song," the psalm calls, telling Israel to "rejoice in him that made him" with dancing, timbrel, and harp (Psalm 149:1-3). "For the LORD taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation" (Psalm 149:4). The psalm ends with the harder picture of the saints executing "vengeance upon the heathen" and binding their kings, calling it "honour" for all his saints (Psalm 149:7-9).
Psalms 149.whereWeAre: Psalm 148 called all creation to praise together. Psalm 149 narrows back to Israel, celebrating its maker with dancing, timbrel, and harp, and picturing the saints carrying out judgment with "a twoedged sword in their hand" (Psalm 149:3,6). Psalm 150 then closes the Psalter with one final, unrestricted call for everything that breathes to praise the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Is called to rejoice in its maker with dancing and song, and to carry out the judgment written against the nations (Psalm 149:2-3,9).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Takes pleasure in his people and beautifies the meek with salvation (Psalm 149:4).

keyThemes.explanation: Israel is called to praise with dancing, timbrel, and harp.
The saints are pictured executing vengeance and binding kings with chains.
Carrying out the judgment written is called an honour for all the LORD's saints.

Psalms 150.summary: "Praise God in his sanctuary: praise him in the firmament of his power," the psalm begins, calling for praise "according to his excellent greatness" (Psalm 150:1-2). It names instrument after instrument, "the sound of the trumpet... the psaltery and harp... the timbrel and dance... stringed instruments and organs... the loud cymbals... the high sounding cymbals" (Psalm 150:3-5). The whole book of Psalms ends, "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD" (Psalm 150:6).
Psalms 150.whereWeAre: Psalm 149 called Israel to praise with dancing and song. Psalm 150 closes the whole book of Psalms with one unrestricted call, naming trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, and cymbals before ending, "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD" (Psalm 150:3-6). The book of Proverbs follows, turning from this closing praise to practical wisdom for daily life.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is praised for his excellent greatness and mighty acts by every instrument and everything that has breath (Psalm 150:1-2,6).

keyThemes.explanation: Praise is called for according to God's mighty acts and excellent greatness.
Every kind of instrument, from trumpet to cymbals, is named as a means of praise.
The Psalter closes by calling everything that has breath to praise the LORD.
